blueprint_topic: Management of Care — escalation through public-health systems when an event may have cross-border significance
stem: A nurse caring for a recently arrived international traveler identifies an unusual cluster of findings that may represent a significant communicable-disease event. Which action best reflects the nurse's role in a coordinated public-health response?

options.A: Follow facility and jurisdictional reporting procedures promptly so designated public-health authorities can assess the event and coordinate further notification if needed.
options.B: Contact WHO directly with the client's identifying information so WHO can determine which domestic control measures the facility should implement.
options.C: Wait for an international emergency declaration before reporting because cross-border coordination begins after WHO formally classifies the event.
options.D: Manage the event within the facility until the causative organism is confirmed because international reporting frameworks do not address early signals.

rationale: A is correct. The International Health Regulations (IHR) establish national and international mechanisms for surveillance, assessment, information sharing, notification, and response to public-health events that may cross borders. At the bedside, the RN's appropriate role is to use facility and applicable jurisdictional reporting pathways so designated public-health authorities can assess the signal and determine whether further national or IHR notification is required. B is incorrect because routine bedside reporting does not bypass domestic public-health systems, and WHO does not have authority to compel domestic clinical or public-health measures. C is incorrect because IHR surveillance, assessment, and information-sharing functions operate before a public health emergency of international concern or pandemic emergency is declared. D is incorrect because early signals may require assessment and reporting before definitive organism confirmation; cross-border frameworks are designed in part to detect and assess potentially significant events early.
educational_objective: When a potentially significant communicable-disease event is identified, the RN should promptly use facility and jurisdictional public-health reporting pathways so designated authorities can assess, escalate, and coordinate cross-border notification when appropriate.
source_document_title: International Health Regulations (2005), as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024; Amended International Health Regulations Enter into Force; Q&A: International Health Regulations: amendments
source_version_date: Current amended IHR text since September 19, 2025 for States Parties to which the 2024 amendments apply; WHO news release September 19, 2025 notes 11 of 196 States Parties rejected the 2024 amendments; current WHO pages accessed 2026-08-20
source_locator: WHO International Health Regulations topic page — WHO functions under the IHR include global public-health surveillance and assessment of significant events, dissemination of public-health information, technical assistance, support for national surveillance/response capacity, and PHEIC determination when required. WHO September 19, 2025 news release — IHR guide States Parties' rights and obligations concerning cross-border public-health risks; coordinated global action is critical; National IHR Authorities coordinate implementation; States retain sovereign authority and WHO cannot compel country action; 11 States Parties rejected the 2024 amendments. WHO IHR amendments Q&A — WHO cannot force health measures, lockdowns, or restrictions on a country's population.
source_claim_supported: Potentially significant cross-border public-health events are managed through national surveillance/reporting and international IHR coordination; WHO coordinates and recommends but does not compel domestic measures, and bedside clinicians should use applicable domestic reporting systems rather than bypass them.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the item from an abstract international-law statement into an entry-level RN Management of Care scenario. Removed the 'only' distractor and longest-answer cue, qualified the 2024 amendment currentness because 11 States Parties rejected those amendments, and avoided implying that WHO can direct domestic bedside care.

option_audit.A: Correct; places the RN within facility/jurisdictional reporting channels while preserving public-health escalation and IHR coordination roles.
option_audit.B: Plausible escalation misconception; incorrect because the RN should not bypass domestic reporting systems and WHO cannot compel domestic measures.
option_audit.C: Plausible emergency-threshold misconception; incorrect because surveillance, assessment, and information sharing precede formal emergency declarations.
option_audit.D: Plausible diagnostic-certainty misconception; incorrect because assessment/reporting of significant signals need not wait for definitive organism confirmation.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on always/never/only/all/must-type absolutes.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Options contain comparable operational detail; the key is not uniquely signaled by length.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four options are parallel response/escalation actions tied to the same scenario.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified after WHO-based reread and RN-role narrowing.
